theme: The cup of wrath; false prophets; the yoke of Babylon
readingInstruction: Read Jeremiah 25:1-27:22. Jeremiah announces seventy years of captivity, passes a cup of wrath to the nations, and nearly loses his life for the temple sermon. Then he wears a wooden yoke. Look for what God says about Nebuchadnezzar.
settingTheScene: Chapter 25 dates to 605 BC, the fourth year of Jehoiakim, the year of the Battle of Carchemish when Babylon became the dominant power and Nebuchadnezzar took the first exiles, including Daniel. Chapter 26 records the trial that followed the temple sermon. Chapter 27 jumps to the reign of Zedekiah, with Jeremiah wearing a yoke of straps and bars, a living picture of submission to Babylon.
observation: “For twenty-three years… the word of the LORD has come to me, and I have spoken persistently to you, but you have not listened” (25:3).
“Behold, I will send for all the tribes of the north… and for Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant” (25:9).
“This whole land shall become a ruin and a waste, and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years” (25:11).
“Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath” (25:15).
“You will surely die! … This man deserves the sentence of death” (26:8, 11).
“Behold, I am in your hands. Do with me as seems good and right to you. Only know for certain that if you put me to death, you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves” (26:14-15).
“Make yourself straps and yoke bars, and put them on your neck” (27:2).
“But any nation that will bring its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serve him, I will leave on its own land” (27:11).
interpretation:
Chapter 25 is the summary of Jeremiah’s ministry so far. For twenty-three years he spoke and the people did not listen. Now God declares the sentence: seventy years of Babylonian rule. Remarkably, he calls Nebuchadnezzar “my servant.” The pagan king is a tool in God’s hand, used for his purposes. After the seventy years, Babylon too will be judged. Daniel would later read this passage in prayer (Daniel 9:2).

God then gives Jeremiah a cup of the wine of his wrath to pass to all the nations. The picture is of a drunken stagger. No one is exempt, from Jerusalem to Egypt to Sheshach, a code word for Babylon. Judgment begins with God’s own people (“the city that is called by my name”) and extends to everyone.

Chapter 26 shows what it costs Jeremiah to preach this. The priests and prophets demand his death. But the officials and some elders defend him, pointing to Micah, who prophesied judgment in Hezekiah’s day and was not killed, because the king repented. Jeremiah’s calm defense is moving. He is in their hands, but he warns them not to shed innocent blood. The word of God does not change to suit the listener.

Chapter 27 is the yoke. He wears it publicly and sends models to the neighboring kings. His message: serve Babylon, and live. False prophets say that the vessels of the temple will soon come back. Jeremiah says that they will go. It is the harder message because it is true. Faith here means accepting what God says even when popular prophets say otherwise.
connection: Daniel 9:2 says that Daniel understood from the books the number of years that must pass for the desolation of Jerusalem, “seventy years.” Isaiah 51:17 and Revelation 14:10 use the cup of wrath imagery. Jesus prayed in Gethsemane, “Let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39), and drank it for us. Romans 13:1 says that governing authorities are instituted by God. Acts 5:29 says we must obey God rather than men.
application:
Consider whether you resist a hard message because it is not what you want to hear. Ask God for ears to hear.

Remember that God can use a Nebuchadnezzar. Look for how he is using something you did not choose.

Pray for courage like Jeremiah’s before an angry crowd.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to give you ears to hear his word even when it is hard.
Thank Jesus for drinking the cup of wrath for you.
